analysis.one_liner: Lets the government strip a drug maker's monopoly and license competitors if the US price exceeds prices in five peer countries.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have voided drug monopolies when US prices topped median prices in five peer countries, was referred to committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to review the price of every brand-name drug at least once a year against the median price charged for that drug in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan. Any drug found "excessively priced" would lose its government-granted exclusivities, and the government would issue open licenses letting any company make a cheaper generic or biosimilar version, with the original maker receiving a royalty. It also would have created a public database of price determinations and required manufacturers to report prices, revenues, and research and advertising spending, with fines for false or missing reports. The bill never advanced past its committee referral and died at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs, especially those paying out of pocket or through high cost-sharing, because US prices would be capped at roughly the median of five other wealthy countries. Insurers, employers, and government programs (Medicare, Medicaid) would also see lower drug spending.

how_it_helps.text: Requires HHS to review every brand-name drug at least annually for excessive pricing, with a benchmark of the median price in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan, plus a fallback test based on development costs, patient value, and other factors.

When a drug is found excessively priced, the government voids its exclusivities and grants open, non-exclusive licenses letting any company make the drug, with expedited 8-month review of generic and biosimilar applications.

Lets any person petition HHS for an excessive-price determination, and creates a public database naming every drug, manufacturer, and determination so patients and purchasers can see which prices were flagged.

Requires manufacturers to report prices, revenues, R&D spending, and advertising costs for each brand-name drug annually, with civil penalties of up to 1% of a drug's gross revenue per day for false or missing reports.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would lose monopoly profits whenever their US price exceeds the five-country median, and would face new reporting and penalty obligations. Some argue future drug development incentives would shrink as a result.

drawbacks.text: Stripping exclusivity and granting open licenses when a price is 'excessive' could reduce the expected return on developing new drugs, potentially slowing the pipeline of new medicines — the core objection the pharmaceutical industry would raise.

The royalty regime allows a license only if the licensed product can be sold below the 'excessive price' threshold, meaning generic copies could not legally charge more than the domestic price deemed too high — a demanding constraint that could leave manufacturers litigating rather than competing.

Comparing US prices to the median of five other countries imports those countries' pricing systems into US law by reference; if any reference country changes how it prices drugs, US determinations shift automatically.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit for patients was large — bringing US brand-drug prices in line with the median of five peer countries would mean major savings for people on fixed and modest incomes. The chief cost is a real one: systematically stripping monopolies and licensing drugs at capped royalties could reduce the financial reward for developing new drugs, and the bill's cap tying any royalty to a non-excessive price leaves little room for high prices even for genuinely valuable new medicines. A fairer design might calibrate returns to innovation value while still barring prices far above peer countries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, which never acted on it, so it never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on March 23, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The record shows no further action: no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote for the remainder of the 117th Congress.
A Senate subcommittee under HELP held a hearing on the bill's subject, with the hearing printed as S.Hrg. 117-176, but the bill itself was never advanced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept their US pricing power, since no law limits their prices to peer-country levels. Patients who rely on heavily overpriced drugs gained nothing from this Congress on this front.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push for international reference pricing and monopoly waivers.

for.what_they_did: Opposed government price-setting and patent-waiver proposals of this kind and campaigned against them during the drug-pricing debates of this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Sanders-aligned Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and a divided Senate took no action.

industries.note: The bill would let the government void their exclusivities and license their patents at capped royalties whenever US prices exceed the median of five peer countries, and would impose detailed annual reporting with per-day fines. It directly attacks the pricing power on which brand-drug revenue depends.

Open licenses and expedited review would open a new market for competitors to make drugs the government flags as overpriced. Their interest in more competition runs alongside patients' interest in lower prices.

Lower brand-drug prices would reduce drug spending across public and private plans, though the bill does not directly regulate insurers. Savings would flow partly to premiums and public budgets rather than automatically to patients at the pharmacy counter.
